subject: Copywriting
title: Commitment and Consistency
description: A fast breakdown of Commitment and Consistency for builders.

hook.text: Ask someone if they'll vote, and they're 25% more likely to do it. The verbal commitment creates action.

buildup.text: Cialdini calls it consistency: once people commit to something, they act to stay consistent with that commitment.

discovery.text: Free trial sign-ups work this way. You enter your email, then your card. Each small step locks you in deeper.

twist.text: The foot-in-the-door technique: ask for something small first. Once they say yes, the big ask becomes easier.

climax.text: SaaS onboarding uses micro-commitments. Complete your profile, invite a friend, set a goal. Each step binds tighter.

punchline.text: Small yes leads to big yes. Commitment compounds.

quiz.question: What is the 'foot-in-the-door' technique?
options: Starting with a small request to build to a larger one

details.summary: Once people take a small step in a direction, they feel compelled to continue. This principle — commitment and consistency — is why free trials convert, why 'yes ladders' work in sales, and why getting someone to say 'yes' to small requests paves the way for bigger ones.
details.whyItMatters: Commitment and consistency explain why customer journeys work. Small initial commitments — signing up, downloading, attending — create psychological momentum that makes eventual purchase feel like a natural continuation rather than a new decision.
takeaways: Small initial commitments create psychological momentum toward larger ones
Public commitments are more binding than private ones
The foot-in-the-door technique exploits consistency bias

faq.question: What is the foot-in-the-door technique?
faq.answer: Start with a small, easy request that almost everyone will agree to, then follow with progressively larger requests. Each 'yes' creates a self-image of cooperation, and people act consistently with their self-image. A free trial leads to a monthly plan, which leads to an annual commitment.

faq.question: Why do public commitments work better?
faq.answer: Public commitments activate social accountability. Once you've told others you're doing something — or posted about it online — backing out creates cognitive dissonance and social embarrassment. This is why brands encourage customers to share purchases or goals publicly.
